title: Pulpitis, pulp death & dental abscess
blurb: What happens when decay reaches the pulp: reversible and irreversible pulpitis, pulp necrosis, abscesses, how urgent they are and how they're treated.
question: A patient phones at 8.30 am. A lower molar with a known large cavity kept him awake all night with throbbing pain that was worse lying down. This morning the pain has suddenly stopped, but his cheek is starting to swell. What is probably happening inside the tooth, and what should you do with this call?

teach.body: The pulp is soft tissue full of nerves and blood vessels, boxed in by rigid dentine. When bacteria or their toxins from deep caries reach it, it becomes inflamed: pulpitis. Inflamed tissue normally swells, but the pulp has nowhere to go. Pressure builds and squeezes the blood vessels entering through the tiny apical foramen. That's why pulpitis can be so painful, and why an inflamed pulp may die. The dentist diagnoses; your job is to record symptoms accurately and get the patient seen with the right urgency.

steps.sub: Bacteria and toxins approach the pulp

steps.label: Reversible pulpitis

steps.label: Pulp necrosis
steps.sub: The pulp dies; pain may suddenly ease

steps.label: Periapical abscess

values: Keeps them awake; worse lying down

teach.h: Pulp death and the false recovery
teach.body: When the pulp dies (necrosis), its nerves stop working, so the pain may suddenly stop. Patients often think the problem has gone. It hasn't. The dead pulp is now an infected space, and bacteria pass out through the apical foramen into the bone around the root tip. The tooth becomes tender to bite on and may feel 'high'. Over time it may darken to grey. A dead pulp doesn't respond to cold or electric pulp tests.

teach.caption: Infection has travelled down the root canal and out through the apex, forming a collection of pus in the surrounding bone.
Deep occlusal caries has reached the pulp in each tooth. Infection has spread out from the root into the surrounding bone and gum, forming pus (yellow) with inflammation (red) around it.

rows.label: Swelling
values: Yes; may spread to the face

rows.label: Tooth
values: Very tender to bite; may be mobile

teach.caption: Pus is a mix of bacteria, dead tissue and white blood cells. A sinus is a channel the pus has made to drain onto the gum, which often relieves pain.

root.label: Dental pain or swelling
root.sub: Take details and tell the dentist

teach.caption: Always follow your practice's triage protocol. Swelling that threatens the airway is a medical emergency.

teach.body: The dentist removes the source of infection: draining pus (through the tooth or by incision), then root canal treatment (removing the pulp, cleaning, shaping and filling the canals) or extraction. Antibiotics are not a substitute; they're kept for spreading infection or a patient who is systemically unwell. Untreated infection can spread into bone (osteomyelitis) or the tissues of the face and neck. Your role: record symptoms carefully, alert the dentist promptly, prepare the root canal or extraction set-up, and reassure the patient.

teach.text: Pain that suddenly stops after nights of throbbing toothache does NOT mean the tooth has healed. It usually means the pulp has died, and an abscess may follow. Advise the patient to keep their appointment.

items: Reversible pulpitis: short, sharp pain to a trigger; the pulp can recover once the decay is treated.
Irreversible pulpitis: spontaneous, throbbing, lingering pain, worse lying down; needs root canal treatment or extraction.
Necrosis: pain may suddenly stop; infection then spreads out of the apex.
Acute abscess: pus, swelling, severe pain. Chronic abscess: drains through a sinus (gumboil).
Airway, swallowing or eye involvement: 999 or A&E. Facial swelling or fever: urgent.
Record symptoms accurately and alert the dentist promptly.

summary: You can now explain how deep caries leads to pulpitis, tell reversible from irreversible pulpitis by the pain described, explain why pain can stop when the pulp dies, describe acute and chronic abscesses and how infection spreads, judge how urgently a patient needs to be seen, and outline treatment and your role.

A.q: A patient describes spontaneous, throbbing toothache that keeps them awake and lasts for hours. Which condition does this fit best?
A.why: Spontaneous, lingering, throbbing pain that disturbs sleep is typical of irreversible pulpitis.

whyNot.0: Reversible pulpitis gives short, sharp pain to a trigger that stops quickly.
whyNot.2: Dentine hypersensitivity is a brief sharp pain from exposed dentine, not spontaneous throbbing.
whyNot.3: Gingivitis is usually painless and affects the gums, not the pulp.

A.q: What is the pus in a dental abscess made of?
options: Bacteria, dead tissue and white cells
Fluid leaking from the dentinal tubules
A.why: Pus is a collection of bacteria, broken-down tissue and white blood cells that have come to fight the infection.

whyNot.0: Saliva is not trapped to form pus.
whyNot.1: A blood clot is not pus; pus forms from infection.
whyNot.3: Dentinal fluid is a tiny amount and doesn't form an abscess.

A.q: A patient had severe toothache for days, which suddenly stopped yesterday. Today the gum beside the tooth is swollen. What has most likely happened?
options: The pulp healed and the gum is bruised
A filling has sealed the cavity
The pulp died; an abscess is forming
A.why: Pain stopping suddenly often means the pulp has died. Infection then spreads from the apex and an abscess forms.

whyNot.0: An irreversibly inflamed pulp doesn't heal on its own.
whyNot.1: Gingivitis is a gum inflammation from plaque and doesn't follow toothache like this.
whyNot.2: Nothing has been placed; a cavity can't seal itself.

B.q: Which description best fits REVERSIBLE pulpitis?
options: Pain lingering for hours after cold
Brief sharp pain that stops quickly
Throbbing pain worse when lying down
Spontaneous pain waking them at night
B.why: In reversible pulpitis the pain is short and sharp, triggered by cold or sweet, and stops when the trigger is removed.

whyNot.0: Lingering pain after the trigger suggests irreversible pulpitis.
whyNot.2: Throbbing pain worse lying down suggests irreversible pulpitis.
whyNot.3: Spontaneous night pain suggests irreversible pulpitis.

B.q: A patient has a small, painless 'pimple' on the gum near the root of a heavily filled tooth, which sometimes leaks a salty taste. What is it most likely to be?
options: A sinus draining a chronic abscess
B.why: A chronic abscess often drains through a sinus (gumboil), which is usually painless and may leak pus with a salty taste.

whyNot.1: Aphthous ulcers are painful, shallow ulcers that don't discharge pus.
whyNot.2: A blocked minor salivary gland gives a bluish swelling, usually on the lip, not a discharging spot.
whyNot.3: Gingival overgrowth is enlarged gum, not a discharging spot.

B.q: A patient phones about a dental infection. Their face is very swollen and they are struggling to swallow and breathe. What should happen?
options: Advise painkillers, review in a week
Call 999 or send them to A&E now
B.why: Swelling affecting breathing or swallowing can block the airway, so it is a medical emergency.

whyNot.0: A routine slot is far too late for a threatened airway.
whyNot.3: Mouthwashes won't help a spreading infection affecting the airway.

C.q: Why is irreversible pulpitis often so painful?
options: Enamel nerves are exposed to air
Saliva leaks down into the root canals
C.why: The inflamed pulp can't swell within its rigid dentine walls, so pressure rises on the nerves and blood vessels.

whyNot.1: The periodontal ligament isn't torn in pulpitis.
whyNot.2: Saliva leaking into canals isn't the cause of pulpitis pain.

C.q: If a periapical infection is left untreated it can spread into the jaw bone. What is this called?
C.why: Osteomyelitis is infection of the bone, a serious complication of untreated dental infection.

whyNot.0: Osteoporosis is thinning of bone with age, not infection.
whyNot.2: Osteoarthritis is wear of the joints.
whyNot.3: Osteoradionecrosis is bone death after radiotherapy.

C.q: What definitive treatment is the dentist likely to offer for a tooth with irreversible pulpitis?
options: A temporary dressing and routine recall
C.why: An irreversibly inflamed pulp can't recover, so it must be removed (root canal treatment) or the tooth extracted.

whyNot.1: Antibiotics don't treat pulpitis and can't reach a pulp sealed inside the tooth.
whyNot.2: Fluoride varnish is for early enamel lesions.
whyNot.3: A dressing may be a short-term measure, but it isn't the definitive treatment.

reteach.title: A balloon in a box
reteach.question: Imagine blowing up a balloon inside a small wooden box with one tiny hole. What happens to the balloon, and where does anything escape?

blocks.body: The pulp is the balloon; the dentine is the box. When decay irritates the pulp, it tries to swell, but the box won't stretch. First it complains briefly when poked (reversible). Then the pressure throbs constantly (irreversible). Eventually it's squeezed so hard its blood supply is cut off and it dies, and the pain can go quiet. The infected contents then leak out of the only exit, the tiny hole at the root tip, and pus collects there: an abscess.

steps.label: Inflamed
steps.sub: Pulpitis: pain, first brief, then throbbing

blocks.caption: Caries has reached the pulp: the balloon is now under attack inside its box.

explain.body: The pain tells the story. Reversible: short, sharp, triggered, stops quickly; the pulp can recover once the decay is removed. Irreversible: spontaneous, throbbing, lingering, worse lying down; the pulp must be removed or the tooth extracted.

test.q: A patient says cold water causes a sharp twinge that goes within seconds. Which condition does this pain pattern suggest?
test.why: A short, sharp, triggered pain that stops quickly fits reversible pulpitis.

whyNot.1: Irreversible pulpitis pain lingers or comes on by itself.
whyNot.2: An abscess gives throbbing pain and tenderness to biting.
whyNot.3: A dead pulp can't feel cold at all.

explain.body: If inflammation continues, the pulp's blood supply fails and it dies. The pain may suddenly stop, but infection now spreads out through the apex. The tooth may darken and won't respond to pulp tests.

test.q: Why might a dead (necrotic) tooth not respond to a cold test?
options: The cold test is too weak
test.why: When the pulp dies its nerves die too, so there is nothing left to respond to the stimulus.

whyNot.0: Cold passes through enamel to a living pulp easily.
whyNot.1: The same test gets a response from a healthy tooth.
whyNot.3: The tooth is isolated and dried; saliva isn't the reason.

explain.body: An acute abscess has trapped pus under pressure: severe pain, swelling, a very tender tooth and sometimes fever. A chronic abscess drains through a sinus onto the gum (a gumboil) and may cause little pain.

test.q: Which sign suggests a chronic rather than an acute abscess?
options: A draining sinus on the gum
test.why: In a chronic abscess the pus drains through a sinus, relieving pressure, so pain is often mild.

whyNot.0: Severe throbbing pain is typical of an acute abscess.
whyNot.2: Spreading swelling signals an acute, spreading infection.
whyNot.3: Fever is a sign of acute infection affecting the whole body.

explain.body: Infection is treated by removing its source: drainage, then root canal treatment or extraction. Antibiotics are kept for spreading infection or systemic signs. Airway or swallowing problems mean 999 or A&E.

explain.caption: Root canal treatment set-up: (1) irrigation syringes and solutions, (2) operating microscope, (3) electronic apex locator, (4) rubber dam sheet and clamp, (5) endodontic files and accessories, (6) files in the canals of a molar isolated with rubber dam.

test.q: When are antibiotics usually appropriate for a dental abscess?
options: For every toothache, as a precaution
Only after the tooth is extracted
test.why: Antibiotics support, but don't replace, removing the source of infection. They're used for spreading infection or systemic signs.

whyNot.0: Antibiotics don't help toothache from pulpitis and overuse drives resistance.
whyNot.1: Drainage and removing the cause are the main treatment.
whyNot.3: Extraction usually removes the need for antibiotics, unless infection is spreading.
